processing: No detailed Jingpo method is documented. Pickled teas of this border region are generally fresh or fixed leaf packed airtight, often in bamboo, and left to ferment.
appearance_dry: Pickled teas of this kind are not dry at all: expect moist, dark olive leaf.
appearance_liquor: Usually eaten rather than brewed, so there is no characteristic liquor; a brew from similar sour teas is yellow to amber.
appearance_wet: Moist, soft, dark olive leaves, as is typical of pickled teas.
taste_profile: No tasting record specific to this tea exists. Pickled teas of the region are generally sour and savoury, with a bitter edge.

brewing.notes: Mostly a food, so brewing is the exception. In this region, pickled tea is usually dressed like a salad; a hot infusion is only an approximation.

vintage_note: It is a home or village food, not a retail tea sold by vintage. Nothing is documented about seasons or ageing for this particular tea, and with other pickled teas freshness and clean fermentation matter more than a year on the label.
description:
Jingpo pickled tea is named as a tea food of the Jingpo people of Dehong, in western Yunnan, but very little has been written about it specifically.

The closest well-recorded relative is De'ang sour tea from the same prefecture, where fixed leaf is sealed in bamboo tubes and fermented without air, and the edible kind is ready in about two months. That shows what is usual in the area, not how Jingpo households necessarily do it.

Teas of this family are eaten more than drunk, typically tossed with seasonings or cooked with meat and vegetables. Expect sourness first, with bitterness behind it.

If you meet it in Dehong, ask how it was made and how long it was sealed. Do not assume a jar labelled pickled tea elsewhere is the same thing.
history: Little is documented. No dated account or named maker is on record for Jingpo pickled tea, and it should not be confused with De'ang sour tea, whose making is listed as intangible heritage.
